Last year, I REFUSED to write sales posts. F*cking cringe, man. $498K later, I use my own damn system:

P.R.O.M.O, the one post framework that sells by showing, not selling.

Write your next post without playing cringe roulette ↓

1 – Open with a personal moment + proof point

- Pick one problem your ICP can't shut up about
- Tie it to a real moment, yours or a client's
- Stack the receipt right away

→ "Holy sh*t, my Amazon client just closed 25K from LinkedIn."

2 – Reveal the true problem sitting underneath

- Agitate it so the reader FEELS it too
- Name a myth you can debunk
- Show them what it's costing

→ "Nobody taught you to sell without sounding like a used car salesman."

3 – Tie it to your process or way of working

- Talk about the method you used (yours or a client's)
- Stick to one method that solves the real problem

Less choice = less friction.

→ "So I built a 5-step arc that does the pitching while you tell the story."

4 – Back up your claims with receipts

Drop stats and screenshots where skepticism kicks in. Numbers give them reasons to believe.

→ "Last month she turned down an $8K keynote. The $45K retainer attached to her last talk was a better use of her time."

5 – One CTA that owns the sell

Finish with ONE specific step. Don't ask for comments or LinkedIn will bury your post alive.

→ "Visit my website to join the waitlist. Or don't. I'm not your mom."

This is how I made $498K in sales, all from LinkedIn. My consultant clients LOVE it. One closed €14K after her first P.R.O.M.O post.

Last Thursday, I thought I was dying. It wasn't my asthma. It was a gnawing feeling I hadn't had since my last job:

- Counting which "favors" I'd have to cut that month.

Because back then my body wasn't mine to protect. A boss decided when I worked. A startup swallowed €80K of my unpaid work.

Losing control isn't abstract for me. I've lived it. At school, at work, in rooms where being wired differently got punished.

So when the heat hit and my chest closed up? The panic wasn't about the weather. It was the old feeling. Trapped, without an exit or a say.

I built a business that runs on my rules. And that business booked two scared, overheating people into a cold room without flinching.

That's the freedom nobody writes about on LinkedIn. You book the cold room when your body needs it. Because you can.

My fiancée and I both slept that night. Breathing.

And I remembered I built this so my body would always be mine to protect.

PS: That cold hotel room was paid for by posts. If you want the 3 that booked me clients while I slept, I'll break them down in my €1 workshop tomorrow.

items.content:
Last July, I NEVER knew what the f*ck to write about. 11 mil impressions later, I live and die by ONE rule:

Moments FIRST.

Coaches will sell you the craziest lies to make you sound smart.

"Post educational value." 
"Lead with expertise."
"Find a content pillar."

You don't wanna sound smart. AI can beat you in a flash. Be relatable instead.

For the first time, I'm handing over my entire system:

1/ Start with a moment, not an insight

My life is more boring than yours. I still never run out of things to write about. Some of my stuff last week:

- Me not folding my laundry
- Crying in front of 100 people on a call
- Someone asking if I want to be LinkedIn famous

It's stupidly simple. And it WORKS.

2/ Nail your core message

Once I have my moment, I build a rough skeleton around it.

One I wrote recently: “Yesterday, I ran a workshop breaking down the content that made me €28k. And then I started crying”. 

Only halfway there. But it's a skeleton I can dress up.

3/ Decide the goal + who it's for

I don't buy top, middle, bottom of the funnel. Nobody scrolls LinkedIn thinking "I'm in the consideration phase."

My only 3 buckets:

- Personal: make them feel seen → attracts peers
- Proof: show you can do it → attracts peers + ICP
- Promo: trigger them to act now → converts your ICP

My best angles for each: https://lnkd.in/en9wCxMb

4/ Draft the full post

Now you write. All you need is the perfect STORM:

- Stuck: your hook, a moment tied to a pain point
- Thirst: agitate what happened + why it matters
- Obstacle: the pivot or the villain in your story
- Revelation: what you learned or what changed
- Mirror: callback to the hook

One paragraph per bit, and the post formats itself.

Try it here: https://lnkd.in/eqgnbCQe 

5/ Write your hook

This is your ONLY shot at pulling your audience in. The only way to do it: be specific.

PLACE is my proven method for specific hooks. Pick at least 3 elements and make sure cost is one of them

Steal the system here: https://lnkd.in/eiK5pjcy

6/ Call back to your hook

Your reader wants closure. Write the closer right after the hook so they connect. The only rule?  ONE simple action. 

- A statement if you want authority
- A question if you want engagement
- A soft or hard CTA if you want to sell

While y'all hunt for the perfect angle, your best post already happened.

You just didn't write it down. ✌️

PS: This afternoon, I'm dropping a Claude skill that pulls moments from your life. Newsletter subscribers get it first (hit 'visit website' up top)

items.content:
A 6-figure creator just called me a h00ker. He's right. After seducing 8 million, here are my favorite buyer psych triggers ↓

LinkedIn coaches treat hooks like neurosurgery. Babes, it's patterns with a potty mouth.

I use PLACE to make my hooks stupidly specific. But on top of that? I rotate these 5 buyer psychology triggers to get y'all to do whatever the f*ck I want:

1/ Garden-path effect creates instant investment

Write a first line that reads one way, then flip the meaning with the next.

"[A line that means one thing]. [The turn that reveals you meant another]."

The flip forces a re-read. Someone who just caught the twist feels smart = they keep scrolling.

I use this when I'm about to get vulnerable and need a soft way in. Lures them past their defenses before they realize they're about to feel something.

2/ Expectation subversion gets them in the comments

Name the advice everyone parrots, break it, show the receipts.

"[The rule everyone repeats]. [Your proof it's wrong]. [What you did instead]."

You're picking a fight with a belief they hold. They'll comment to argue or to cheer. 

This one's my chaos gremlin for when I want smoke.

3/ Self-disclosure reciprocity builds trust

Show the win everyone sees, then admit the private cost behind it.

"[The public flex]. [The thing behind it you don't say out loud]."

You go first with something real. They drop their guard because you dropped yours.

FYI, people don't connect with your wins. They connect with what your wins cost you.

4/ Time contrast makes them believe in you

Put two moments side by side. Same you, different chapter.

"At [then], I [low point]. At [now], I [where you are]. [The line that ties them]."

Two timestamps do the selling. The distance you covered is proof it's possible for them too.

Comeback fuel, baby. 

5/ Pratfall effect makes them want to buy

Drop a real number to flex, then pair it with a flaw you're not hiding.

This unemotional man blocked me everywhere within the hour. Said he wouldn't pay. Waved off $83K of unpaid labor like it was pocket change.

Highly profitable, these female instincts. ✌️

items.content:
Your prospects delete your emails
faster than you delete pizza flyers.

The flyer at least targets someone who orders pizza.
Your email targets a job title.

After years in sales, here is the most valuable thing I learned:

Every deal starts with two things.

1. The right keyword, placed as early as possible in your pitch or your email.
2. The right timing.

Let me explain why timing became an obsession for me.
Over the last five years I sold for Deel and for cyber startups.

Deel has several products, and each one matches a precise moment in a company's life cycle. A company opening an office abroad has a need that did not exist a month earlier. Catch that moment and the situation dictates the pitch.

Same in cybersecurity: a fresh fundraise means shipping faster, hiring in waves, and a growing surface to attack.

Knowing this changed nothing about how hard it was.
Catching these moments was fully manual, and honestly discouraging. On 200 cold calls, you land on a good timing once, if you are lucky. Same odds on 500 or 1,000 cold emails.

The technique was right and the job still felt like a lottery.

In 2026, hoping you arrived at the right moment is no longer a strategy you're allowed to have. The tools exist now.

That's what I use lemlist agents for. 

I pick the signals that matter for my business (a fundraise, an office opening, a hiring spree on a specific role) and they scan daily. 

When one fires, the lead lands in my campaign, and the signal tells me both things at once: which words to open with, and that today is the day to reach out.

Since I made the switch, my cold email open rate went from 18% to 61%. And the same shift happened on my cold calls, because opening with the right keyword at the right moment works on the phone even better than in writing.

But the numbers are not even the real change.

I do a third of the volume I used to, and I close more than I ever did, because I spend my weeks talking to people instead of trying to talk to people.

And there is a side effect nobody mentions: confidence. Sending 500 emails into the void and dialing 150 numbers a week where nothing is happening quietly destroys yours. Reaching out where something just happened means getting taken seriously on almost every touch, and that changes how you sell everything.

The volume was never my problem. Arriving after the signature was.

items.content:
I lost more deals to my inbox than to competitors.

Every time my pipeline looked bad, I ran the same ritual. 
Friday night, inbox open, calendar open, scrolling through weeks of calls looking for one thing: the follow-ups I never sent.

And I found them. Every time. 
A great call, a prospect saying "we'll get back to you" or "timing isn't quite right yet", and then nothing. No email. Or one email with the info they asked for, then silence.

Just by reaching back out, I booked meetings and closed deals. Which means the ones I never caught are still out there. Deals I lost without ever knowing they existed.

You can be great at sales and still miss this. Run 7 calls in a day, let one big deal eat your whole week, and things slip. You're human.

I don't run that Friday ritual anymore. I keep Granola open during my calls. 
It's an AI notepad, no bot popping into the meeting, and it takes the notes for me while I stay focused on the prospect.

The second I hang up, it's all there. Clean notes, what I promised to send, and the follow-up already drafted, exactly the way a good follow-up should be. I read it, change a word or two, send.

Even on the days when I'm running from call to call, the follow-up goes out. And a prospect who gets a sharp, personal email minutes after we hang up notices. It says something about how seriously you take their business. 

I'm never going back. The results speak for themselves.

Deals don't die in my inbox anymore.
